Monday: Sharmila's scholarship was delayed again, and the hostel mess fee of 3,000 was due on Friday. She spent the evening scrolling past Parveen's name, cheeks hot. Asking felt like admitting she had failed.
Wednesday: Avoiding it wasn't working; she'd started skipping dinner. On the library steps she said it straight: "Parveen, I need to borrow 3,000 for the mess fee. My scholarship comes on the 20th, and I'll pay you back on the 21st. If that's hard for you, just say no, really." Parveen transferred it that night. "Stop looking so guilty," she said.
The 21st: The scholarship landed at noon. By one, Sharmila had sent the 3,000 back with a message: "Returned. Thank you for trusting me." That evening she bought two plates of momos near the gate. "Not interest," she said. "Just momos." Parveen laughed and took the bigger plate.

qa.a: 3,000, due on Friday.

passage:
Nikita, you're worried about asking Divya for that money? Let me, your Irawati Masi, tell you what I did wrong at your age.
I was twenty, in Pune, learning typing and shorthand. My father's money order was late, and my friend Sushma lent me eighty rupees without a question. Eighty was a lot then. I said, "I'll return it soon." Soon. No date.
Then the money order came, and there were books to buy, and I told myself next month. And the month after that I started taking the other staircase so I wouldn't meet her. Imagine. Sushma hadn't asked once, and I was hiding like a thief.
Finally she came to my room and said, "I don't care about the eighty. I miss you." I cried and gave it back that same day, from the money for my new sandals.
So when you ask Divya, say the amount, say the date, and keep it. The money is small. The friendship isn't.

qa.q: How much did Sushma lend Irawati?
qa.a: Eighty rupees.

qa.q: Why did Irawati start taking the other staircase?
qa.a: She felt guilty and ashamed about the unpaid loan and avoided Sushma rather than face her.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Irawati's story, and what did she choose then?
qa.a: Sushma coming to her room to say she missed her; Irawati returned the money that same day.

qa.q: How did Sushma see the unpaid loan?
qa.a: She cared far more about the lost friendship than the eighty rupees, and simply missed Irawati.

grounding: Illustrates borrowing from a friend without a clear date, avoiding them as the debt sours the friendship, and repairing it by repaying.

I'm writing because if I say this in person, I'll either shout or cry.
In August I told you, and only you, that I was repeating the semester because I kept freezing in exams. Yesterday three people in the lab asked me if I was "okay now". One of them said you'd mentioned it at Gautam's party.
I felt exposed, standing there in my lab coat with everyone looking. I was furious. For an hour I wanted to tell the whole class what you once told me about your brother. I'm not going to. I don't want to become that.
But you need to know: it hurt, and it changed things. I'm not ending our friendship in this letter, and I'm not pretending it's fine either. I'll be slower to share things with you now. If you want to talk, I'll listen, once, on Saturday in the reading room.

Nandini, you asked why I'm so careful with other people's secrets. I'm Shalini aunty to you now, but at twenty-one I was just a hostel girl who liked being interesting.
My friend Leena told me she had failed one paper and was hiding it from her parents. One night, bored, I told it to three girls in the common room. For attention, nothing else.
When Leena found out, she asked me why. And I said the stupidest thing: "It's not a big deal, everyone fails a paper. You're overreacting." I made it her problem.
She moved rooms the next month. Years later I wrote her a proper apology, no excuses. She replied kindly. But the friendship never came back, and I understand why.
If you ever do what I did, own it the same day. Say sorry without a "but". And then let the other person decide how close to stand.

qa.q: What secret did Leena tell Shalini?

qa.q: Why did Shalini tell the secret in the common room?

qa.a: When Leena asked why; instead of calling it "not a big deal", Shalini should have owned it and apologised without excuses right away.

qa.q: How did Leena experience Shalini's response?
qa.a: As a second hurt: being told she was overreacting after her secret was spread, which is why she moved rooms.

grounding: Illustrates betraying a friend's confidence for attention and the harm of minimising it, with the lesson to own it and apologise without excuses.

Last month Pradeep dropped Shreya as his doubles partner two days before the zonal trials, by message, to play with a stronger player. It hurt her; she missed a week of practice.
Today Pradeep came to her after drills and apologised. I was restringing rackets nearby and saw it. Shreya listened with her arms folded, then said, "I forgive you. I'm not carrying this anymore. But I'm not ready to be partners again."

Vinita sent me a long message tonight. Sorry, sorry, sorry. For telling Dhruv, of all people, that I had a crush on him, "as a joke", in front of the whole lab.
It's been three weeks. The old me would've replied "haha it's fine" and gone back to normal. That's what I did in school, and it always came back later as a stomach ache.

Last term, Shankar and Gauri both came to me on the same evening, about the same thing: who deserved the lead name on our robotics poster. Shankar texted, "You saw who stayed till midnight. Back me up." Gauri called: "You know the design was mine."

On the college bus from the villages outside Kottayam, the back seats had a game: whenever Chandrika from the dairy family got on, someone would hold their nose and moo softly. Jomon always laughed. It was easier than being the one who didn't.
On Monday Chandrika got on with her hands tucked into her dupatta, and Binu started the moo. Jomon's laugh came out, then stuck halfway. He remembered his own first week, when the same boys called him "rubber-tapper's son" until he stopped wearing his father's old shirt.
He didn't make a speech. When Binu nudged him to moo too, he said, "Nah, leave it," and moved to the empty seat two rows ahead, near Chandrika. He asked if the chemistry practical was still on Thursday.
She glanced at him warily. "Yes. Thursday."
Behind them, the mooing trailed off. Binu called him boring. Jomon looked out at the rubber trees and let him.

qa.q: What did the back seats do whenever Chandrika got on?
qa.a: Held their noses and mooed softly.

qa.q: Why did Jomon's laugh stick halfway on Monday?
qa.a: He remembered being called "rubber-tapper's son" and felt uncomfortable and ashamed, recognising how it feels on the other side.

qa.q: How did Jomon quietly refuse to join in?
qa.a: He said "Nah, leave it", moved to the seat near Chandrika and talked to her normally about the practical.

qa.q: How might Chandrika see Jomon sitting near her?
qa.a: Warily at first, unsure whether it's another trick, but possibly relieved when the mooing trails off.

grounding: Illustrates laughing along at someone's expense, noticing how it feels from the other side, and quietly refusing to continue.
